name: Breaking stigma on mental health in learning institutions

content.title: Breaking stigma on mental health in learning institutions
content.summary: AKU Tanzania hosts seminar to raise awareness on mental health and share lived experiences

media.caption: Participants engaging in a group activity during the Mental Health Research Seminar Series held at the Dar es Salaam campus in Tanzania.
media.alt: Breaking stigma on mental health in learning institutions

content.text: In today's fast-paced world, mental health has emerged as a critical topic deserving attention and exploration. Over 100 faculty, staff, students and alumni from Aga Khan University's Institute for Educational Development, East Africa (IED,EA) and School of Nursing and Midwifery, East Africa (SONAM,EA) convened for a research seminar series on mental health.  The seminar was held to raise awareness on mental health, encourage reflection and empower search of knowledge on mental health.

Mental health encompasses emotional, psychological, and social wellbeing, influencing how we think, feel, and act. Contrary to popular belief, mental health is not limited to those experiencing mental illnesses. It is an integral part of every individual's life, shaping their overall wellness and quality of life. Research has shown that one out of four people experience mental health struggles in Tanzania.

"There is no health without mental health. It is a basic human right and is crucial to personal, community and socio-economic development. Mental illness is nothing to be ashamed of, it is a medical problem, just like heart disease or diabetes," said Dr Tumbwene Mwasisya, Associate Professor in Psychiatry and Mental Health at SONAM, EA.

Historically, mental health has been masked by stigma and misunderstanding, often causing individuals to suffer in silence. A lived experience was shared by Lucy Rweyemamu, Senior Manager at IED, EA. She narrated how a loved one battled depression from being bullied at school and the inability of her parents to distinguish her actions and reactions as behavioural and not mental illness. From the story, the participants were able to draw scenarios of what challenges she encountered and what could have been done in such a situation. The story further aroused interest for research on how teachers can contribute to stop bullying in schools, how teachers can help shape and build resilient mental health systems in schools and the role of social media in overcoming mental health stigma.

However, times are changing, and societies are actively dismantling these barriers. People from all walks of life are coming forward to share their stories, encouraging open conversations and promoting empathy. These courageous voices are paving the way for a more inclusive and understanding world, where seeking support for mental health concerns is seen as a sign of strength, not weakness.

"The places where we spend a lot of time including home, work, school, and even socially can have a significant impact on our mental well-being. In most cases, people are trying to fit in to conform to the standards of their environment or society at large. When this happens, it can lead to increased stress, depression, anxiety and other negative reactions. Consequently, the pressure from the environment can have a detrimental impact on one's mental health. Therefore, we all must have empathy and create a safe place and environment at large where one would feel comfortable to share their challenges and stories," said Lucy Rweyemamu.

By embracing the importance of mental wellbeing and fostering an environment of understanding, we can collectively empower individuals to prioritize their mental health. The Aga Khan University is committed to advocating for the wellbeing of its employees and students through inclusion of mental health in the teaching and learning curriculum.  Additionally, there will be regular sensitization seminars on mental health for staff and faculty.
